# LEADING THE SAME CHANGE IN DIFFERENT PLACES
## A regional adaptation guide for a global empowerment and culture-change initiative

**Guidance note and decision paper for the Executive Sponsor, Regional Presidents, Global Function Heads and HR/Transformation leads | v2.0**
*(Supersedes v1.0. The country-by-country field annex, translation glossary and works-council briefing pack are Annexes A–C and are not required to take the decisions in §16.)*

**What is being asked of the reader.** Six things, and nothing else:

1. **Approve the four invariant outcomes (I-1 to I-4) and their thresholds** as written in §1 — including the decision classes in §1.3, which are the only definition of "empowerment" this programme will use.
2. **Approve the [I]/[A]/[L] decision-rights split** in §0.2 and the governance and arbitration route in §12, including the stop conditions.
3. **Name, by [Month 0 + 14 days], one accountable regional owner per region** at Regional President minus one, and confirm they meet the capability bar in §6.1.
4. **Sign the displacement offsets in §14** — each region confirming in writing what stops so the programme's demand on manager attention is funded rather than assumed.
5. **Approve the HR-systems workstream (§10) as invariant**, accepting that promotion, rating and incentive criteria change in all regions on the same schedule.
6. **Approve €[2.1]m programme cost plus €[350]k contingency** for Wave 1 and 2 (§14.4). Wave 3 funding is not sought now; it is released at Gate 2 (§13.3).

---

## The recommendation in one paragraph

A global empowerment initiative fails in two symmetrical ways: HQ exports its own cultural idiom as if the idiom were the change (perfect adoption at headquarters, polite non-adoption everywhere else), or every region redefines "empowerment" until it means what it was already doing (twelve programmes, one name, no transferable capability). The defence against both is to fix the **outcomes** globally and delegate the **methods** regionally, deciding which is which *before* rollout rather than arguing about it in month nine. We therefore define empowerment behaviourally, not lexically — four observable outcomes (§1) built on an explicit three-class decision-rights taxonomy — and treat everything else as adaptable or local. The central non-obvious point, which should reshape how most of our regional leaders act, is that **empowerment is not the opposite of hierarchy**: autonomy requires a visible, credible grantor, and in most of our markets the only person who can grant it is the senior figure being asked to "flatten" (§2). The second non-obvious point is that the strongest predictor of whether this works at a given site is not national culture but **local consequence memory** — what actually happened to the last person who disagreed or failed there (§3.1). Two populations decide the outcome and both are currently under-served by change programmes of this kind: **regional leaders**, who must be selected and held to a capability bar rather than merely briefed (§6), and **middle managers**, whose status is what the initiative appears to attack and who must therefore be re-contracted, not exhorted (§7). None of it survives contact with an unchanged reward system, so HR-systems alignment is invariant, not optional (§10). Two claims in this paper are load-bearing and are deliberately **not** asserted: that our Wave 1 sites have sufficient consequence-memory headroom for I-2 and I-3 to be achievable by messaging plus mechanism, and that our middle managers will accept the re-contract in §7 at the price offered. §15 states in advance what result would stop or de-scope the programme.

---

## §0 How to use this document

### 0.1 How to read the figures and claims

Three kinds of statement appear here, tagged on first use. Confusing them is how change programmes come to believe their own assumptions.

| Tag | Type | Example | Certainty | Resolved by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **[V]** | **Verifiable fact** | Codetermination rights, consultation thresholds, data-protection limits on surveys, nationalisation quotas | Should be *certain* — verify, never estimate | Gate 0, by employment counsel per jurisdiction |
| **[R]** | **Researchable finding** | Escalation rates, consequence memory, middle-manager sentiment, English-proficiency asymmetry | Diagnostic evidence: directional, site-specific, ±[20]% | Gate 0, by the §4 diagnostic |
| **[D]** | **Design target** | Thresholds, cadences, wave sizes, budget, timelines | A choice we are making, not a fact we are discovering | Gate 1, by the Executive Sponsor |

No number in this paper is a fact unless tagged **[V]**. Every threshold is **[D]** and every one is filled in; there are no blanks to be resolved later by whoever is holding the pen.

### 0.2 The decision-rights taxonomy, applied to every element in this document

| Tag | Meaning | Who decides | Change process |
|---|---|---|---|
| **[I] Invariant** | Identical everywhere. Non-negotiable. | Executive Sponsor | Documented exception, Board-level only, time-limited |
| **[A] Adaptable** | The *outcome* is fixed; the *method* is regional | Regional President, logged in the adaptation register (§12.2) | **Documented, not requested** — see §12.2 for what that means operationally |
| **[L] Local** | Wholly delegated to country/site | Country leader | No approval, no logging |

Every section heading below carries a tag. Every table row in the operational sections carries a tag. If an element is untagged, treat it as not ready to roll out and escalate under §12.4.

### 0.3 Scope

| In scope | Out of scope |
|---|---|
| Decision-rights devolution, dissent, error-handling and adaptive routine (I-1 to I-4) | Restructuring, delayering, span-of-control redesign |
| Regional leadership capability, selection and accountability for these outcomes | Executive succession beyond the named programme roles |
| Middle-manager role re-contract | Grading and job-architecture reform beyond §10.3 |
| HR-systems alignment where it directly rewards or punishes I-1 to I-4 | Total-reward benchmarking, pensions, mobility policy |
| Legal and codetermination constraints on the above | Any labour-relations negotiation not triggered by this programme |

**Explicitly out:** this is not a cost programme and must never be introduced as one. If headcount reduction occurs in any region within [6] months either side of that region's launch, the programme is suspended in that region (§15, R-2). Empowerment announced beside redundancies is heard as offloading, permanently.

### 0.4 The resourcing rule — and its enforcement

**Every commitment made to this initiative consumes manager attention, and manager attention is already fully allocated.** No activity appears in this paper without a named owner, a duration, and a stated displacement — what stops, what is deferred, or what budget buys the capacity. §14 does this arithmetically for every activity, including the diagnostic in §4. A workstream with no stated displacement cost has not been designed; it has been wished for. Applied to this document itself: if the Board approves the outcomes but not the displacements in §14, the correct decision is to approve Wave 1 only, at one-third scope.

### 0.5 A caution on the regional material in §5 — and why a country cut still appears

National-culture frameworks (Hofstede; the GLOBE studies; Erin Meyer's *The Culture Map*) are **descriptive heuristics with known and serious limits**, not predictive instruments:

- **Aggregation-level error.** Hofstede's dimensions were derived from a single-employer survey population (IBM, late 1960s–early 1970s) and describe country means. Applying a country mean to an individual or a single site is a recognised misuse — McSweeney's critique of the method remains unanswered in the practitioner literature.
- **Sample mismatch.** Our employees are not a national sample. They are urban, educated, English-capable, self-selected into a multinational, and in several markets a majority-expatriate workforce.
- **Within- versus between-country variation.** Our working assumption is that variation between two of our own sites in one country will often exceed variation between country means. This is tagged **[R]** — it is a hypothesis the §4 diagnostic will test in the first three markets, not a finding.
- **Staleness.** Generational change in India, Korea, Greater China, the Gulf and Central Europe has plausibly outrun the frameworks' vintage. Also **[R]**.

**So why does §5 contain regional material at all?** Because a first hypothesis has to come from somewhere, and the cheapest available prior is the observed regional pattern. §5 is therefore reorganised from v1.0: it is structured **by the diagnostic variables of §3**, with regions appearing as *illustrations of a variable profile* rather than as units of analysis. Each entry is **[R]** — a question to test in week one, not a fact. A regional leader who reports "our site does not match the profile" has done the exercise correctly, and the diagnostic memo (§4) overrides §5 without appeal.

---

## §1 What "empowerment" must mean before it can be translated **[I]**

### 1.1 The word is the first risk

"Empowerment" is a positive abstraction in English. Translated literally it frequently arrives as one of:

- ***"You are now on your own."*** Abandonment — acute where managerial protection is a valued part of the leadership contract (Latin America, much of South and Southeast Asia).
- ***"Your manager's authority is being reduced."*** A status threat that mobilises the exact layer we depend on (§7).
- ***"More work, same grade, same pay."*** Offloading — the default reading wherever headcount is tight.
- ***"Another HQ campaign."*** Cynicism, wherever a decade of initiatives has taught it.

The programme is therefore defined by observable outcomes and by the mechanism in §1.3, and no regional expression may substitute for them.

### 1.2 The four invariant outcomes **[I]**

| # | Invariant outcome | Instrument | Threshold, month 12 **[D]** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **I-1** | **Class B decisions are closed at the lowest competent level** (§1.3) | Repeat decision archaeology (§4.1), quarterly, on a random sample of [20] closed decisions per site | ≥[70]% of Class B decisions closed without escalation, from a Wave 1 baseline we expect near [35]% **[R]** |
| **I-2** | **Disagreement travels upward without career cost** | Composite index, §11.3 — archival decision-reversal log plus third-party-collected sentiment, never manager-reported | ≥[15]% of logged Class A/B decisions materially changed by input from below the deciding level; sentiment index +[12] points over baseline |
| **I-3** | **Honest error is survivable** | Audit of leader behaviour, not of showcased failures (§1.4) | ≥[90]% of reviewed good-faith failures closed with no individual sanction and a documented process change; [100]% of Wave-1 regional leaders have personally published one "what I got wrong" account |
| **I-4** | **Adaptation is routine** | Team-level working-method change log | ≥[75]% of teams have changed at least one of their own working methods per quarter without upward approval, for two consecutive quarters |

### 1.3 The decision classes — the substance behind the slogan **[I] for the taxonomy, [A] for the thresholds**

Empowerment that does not name decisions is a poster. Three classes, defined globally; monetary thresholds indexed regionally by the Regional President within a ±[40]% band **[A]**:

| Class | Content | Devolution |
|---|---|---|
| **A — Reserved** | Safety; legal and regulatory commitments; capital above €[250]k; pricing outside approved band; external brand and sustainability claims; hiring above grade [M3]; anything creating precedent across regions | **Never devolved.** Naming these protects the rest. |
| **B — Devolvable (the whole target of I-1)** | Operating spend to €[25]k; method and process change within a team; supplier selection from the approved list; customer concession to €[10]k; scheduling and resourcing within budget; hiring to grade [M2] within approved plan; local vendor and tooling choices | **Devolved by named, written, publicly issued grant** (§9.2) |
| **C — Already local** | Anything a team already decides without asking | No action — but audit for shadow escalation |

I-1's test is deliberately *not* "a decision-rights map exists." Documentation measures documentation. The map (a Class B grant register per team) is a prerequisite; the measured outcome is the escalation rate found by decision archaeology.

### 1.4 Why I-3 is written as it is **[I]**

v1.0 required "one visible case per region where a good-faith failure was reviewed without sanction, and the learning published." That metric corrupts under pressure: regions would curate a harmless failure and publish it. It also collides with **[V]** limits on publishing employee-identifiable conduct reviews in Germany, France, the Netherlands and any EU jurisdiction under GDPR Art. 6/9, and with works-council rights where publication has disciplinary implication.

The rewrite measures the **leader's** behaviour and the **system's** response, not an exhibit:

- Every good-faith failure above a materiality line gets a review whose written output is **process and decision-focused, anonymised at individual level** — no names, no attributable conduct findings.
- Sanction data is audited in aggregate by Internal Audit **[I]**, not self-reported by the region.
- The one *personal* disclosure required is from the senior leader themselves — a leader's own account of a decision they got wrong. That is safe (the discloser holds the power), non-extractive, and it is the single most efficient signal available (§9.3).

### 1.5 What is not fixed

| Element | Tag |
|---|---|
| Who grants authority, how visibly, in what forum | **[A]** |
| Whether dissent flows in the meeting, the pre-meeting, a 1:1, or in writing | **[A]** |
| How error is discussed, and by whom | **[A]** |
| Pace of adoption within the Gate schedule (§13) | **[A]** |
| Vocabulary, programme name, translation | **[L]** |
| Ceremony, symbols, recognition mechanisms, training delivery format | **[L]** |

> **Design implication:** most markets should give the programme a **local name**. A single global brand name is a vanity. What must be global is I-1 to I-4, the decision classes, and the measurement.

---

## §2 Empowerment is not the opposite of hierarchy **[I] as a principle**

The most common HQ error is to assume the initiative requires flattening. It does not — and in much of the company, flattening would remove the only available instrument.

**The mechanism, stated generally:** autonomy is only usable if the person exercising it believes it will be **defended**. Belief requires a **grantor** who is (a) visible, (b) credible to that employee, and (c) seen to bear the cost when a delegated decision goes wrong. Three variables follow, and they are what actually differ between our sites — not "how hierarchical people are":

| Variable of the grant | Range observed | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **Who is a credible grantor** | The direct manager / the site's senior figure / a respected technical authority / the works council or union as co-signatory / a visible HQ sponsor | Grant issued by the wrong figure is not believed and will not be used |
| **How visible the grant must be** | Private confirmation is sufficient ↔ public, specific, named announcement is required | Where public grant is required, quiet delegation reads as a trap and employees correctly decline it |
| **How the grantor's cost-bearing is demonstrated** | Verbal support ↔ the grantor publicly absorbs the first failure | Undemonstrated cost-bearing collapses the grant on first error |

**Board decision paper | v2.0**

**Decision sought:** approval of the two-track structure, the beachhead selection method and its result, the positioning boundary, the channel sequence, the origin rule in §6.2, and **€290k (plus €45k contingency) to fund Gate 0**. Country choice becomes irrevocable only at Gate 1.

## The recommendation in one paragraph

Expansion into "a new region" is two decisions, not one. **Demand entry** and **supply entry** have different criteria, different clock speeds, different failure modes and different owners; fusing them into a single geography is how mid-sized brands lose margin in both. We propose a **Demand Track** entering **Japan** as beachhead — chosen on the scored criteria in §3.2, not asserted — with **South Korea opened by trigger, not by date** (§3.5); and a **Supply Track** qualifying **Vietnam** as a new manufacturing origin while retaining **Portugal and Turkey** as nearshore replenishment and **India as a source of certified organic fibre and yarn only**. The two tracks meet at one technical point and it is not the one an earlier draft claimed: preference eligibility is governed by **rules of origin, not by where the sewing happens**, which produces a single hard rule — **fibre and yarn may cross borders; fabric may not** (§6.2). Positioning is *not* "well-made sustainable basics"; Uniqlo and Muji own that ground in Japan permanently and will out-execute us on it forever. We enter as a **provable-longevity** brand — garments sold with their own evidence and their own repair — at a price architecture that never competes with either (§4). Channels are sequenced credibility-first and capital-last: distributor and wholesale before any entity, lease or local payroll, so that a failed entry costs a contract rather than a balance sheet (§5, §10.3). Two claims in this paper are load-bearing and are therefore **not** asserted: that Vietnamese vertical certified-organic fabric capacity exists at our quality and volume, and that Japan out-scores Korea on willingness-to-pay for provenance. Gate 0 exists to test exactly those two things, and §3.6 states in advance what result would flip the recommendation.

### 0.1 How to read the figures

Three kinds of number appear here, tagged on first use. Confusing them is the main way strategy papers mislead their own authors.

| Tag | Type | Example | How certain | Resolved |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **[V]** | **Verifiable fact** | Tariff line, rule of origin, labelling statute, tax threshold | Should be *certain* — verify, never estimate | Gate 0, by counsel and a customs broker |
| **[R]** | **Researchable quantity** | Import volumes, competitor retail prices, wholesale margin norms, CAC | Trade and customs data: ±[15]%. **Niche premium segment sizing: ±[40]% at best** | Gate 0, by field research |
| **[D]** | **Design target** | Our Year-3 revenue, channel mix, vendor count, price points | A choice we are making, not a fact we are discovering | Gate 1, by this Board |

Everything touching tariff preference, rules of origin, labelling or entity law is **[V]** — a Gate 0 verification item, not a settled fact in this paper. Preference regimes phase down, graduate and expire; §6.5 prices that risk rather than merely noting it.

### 0.2 In scope / out of scope

| In scope | Out |
|---|---|
| One new demand region, entered through one beachhead country | Wholesale expansion inside existing EU markets |
| One new manufacturing origin, plus fibre sourcing | Renegotiating existing Portuguese/Turkish terms |
| Substantiation infrastructure (required by EU law regardless) | M&A, licensing, franchising |
| The organisational capacity to run both without degrading the core | Category extension beyond market-fit adaptation |

### 0.3 The rule of this document

**Every commitment to the new market carries a stated cost to the core business** — attention, working capital, or inventory risk. This is not a slogan; it is enforced numerically in §2.4 (attention budget) and §8.3 (working-capital draw). A line item in this paper without a named cost to the core has not been thought through.

Baseline, to be confirmed at Gate 0: revenue €[78]m **[R]**, gross margin [58]%, EBITDA [8.5]%, [210] FTE, [62]% of revenue in DE/NL/Nordics, wholesale/DTC split [55/45].

---

## §1 The three questions that matter

| Wrong question | Right question |
|---|---|
| Which country next? | What are we short of — customers, margin, capacity, or credibility — and which geography is the cheapest source of *that specific thing*? |
| Where can we sell sustainable clothing? | Where is sustainability a **purchase driver** rather than a **tiebreaker**? |
| Where can we manufacture more cheaply? | What is our **landed cost after duty, freight, lead-time inventory, defect rate and audit overhead** — and does the preference actually apply to *our* bill of materials? |

**Corollary 1 — cheap labour is not cheap.** FOB price is the smallest and least reliable term in landed cost. A [15]% FOB saving **[D]** is erased by an [11.5]% MFN duty if origin fails **[V]**, by a [4]-week lead-time extension financed as inventory, by a [2]-point defect rate, or by one labour finding that costs a retail listing. Sourcing decisions are landed-cost-after-risk decisions.

# LEADING THE SAME CHANGE IN DIFFERENT PLACES
## A regional adaptation guide for a global empowerment and culture-change initiative

**Guidance note for the Executive Sponsor, Regional Presidents and HR/Transformation leads | v1.0**

---

## §0 How to use this document

### 0.1 The single distinction the whole document rests on

A global culture initiative fails in one of two symmetrical ways:

| Failure | Mechanism | Symptom at month 9 |
|---|---|---|
| **Over-standardisation** | HQ exports its own cultural idiom as if it were the change itself | Perfect compliance in the HQ region, polite non-adoption everywhere else |
| **Over-localisation** | Every region redefines "empowerment" until it means whatever it was already doing | Twelve programmes, one name, no transferable capability |

The defence against both is to decide *in advance* which elements are fixed globally and which are deliberately delegated. Everything in this document is therefore tagged:

| Tag | Meaning | Who decides | Change process |
|---|---|---|---|
| **[I] Invariant** | Identical everywhere. Non-negotiable. | Executive Sponsor | Board-level exception only |
| **[A] Adaptable** | The *outcome* is fixed; the *method* is regional | Regional President, with HQ visibility | Documented, not requested |
| **[L] Local** | Wholly delegated to the country/site | Country leader | No approval needed |

If a leader cannot say which of the three a given element is, the element is not ready to roll out.

### 0.2 The resourcing rule

**Every commitment made to this initiative consumes manager attention, and manager attention is already fully allocated.** No new behaviour is introduced anywhere in this programme without naming what stops, what is deferred, or what budget replaces it. Section 12 enforces this numerically. A workstream with no stated displacement cost has not been designed; it has been wished for.

### 0.3 A caution on the regional material in §5

The regional profiles are **starting hypotheses, not facts.** National-culture frameworks (Hofstede, GLOBE, Meyer) describe population averages and are prone to three errors when applied to a company:

1. **Ecological fallacy.** Within-country variation in management style usually exceeds between-country variation. A Munich R&D lab and a Munich sales office differ more than Munich and Milan R&D labs.
2. **Sample mismatch.** Our employees are not a national sample. They are urban, educated, English-capable, self-selected into a multinational, and in several markets a majority-expatriate workforce.
3. **Staleness.** Generational change in India, Korea, China, the Gulf and Poland has moved faster in fifteen years than these frameworks have.

Use §5 to form a question, then verify it locally in the diagnostic (§4). Treating §5 as settled truth reproduces exactly the stereotyping the initiative is meant to dissolve.

---

## §1 What "empowerment" must mean before it can be translated

The word is the first risk. In English, "empowerment" is a positive abstraction. Translated literally it frequently arrives as one of:

- *"You are now on your own"* — abandonment, especially where managerial protection is a valued part of the leadership contract
- *"Your manager's authority is being reduced"* — a status threat that mobilises the exact layer we depend on
- *"More work, same grade, same pay"* — offloading
- *"Another HQ campaign"* — where a decade of programmes has taught cynicism

Therefore the programme is defined **behaviourally, not lexically**. The following four outcomes are **[I] Invariant**; every regional expression must produce them, and no regional expression may substitute for them.

| # | Invariant outcome | Observable test |
|---|---|---|
| **I-1** | **Decision rights are explicit and pushed to the lowest competent level** | A named decision-rights map exists per team; ≥X% of a defined decision class is closed without escalation |
| **I-2** | **Disagreement can be surfaced upward without career cost** | Employees can name a recent instance where a decision changed because someone junior objected |
| **I-3** | **Honest error is survivable** | At least one visible case per region where a good-faith failure was reviewed without sanction, and the learning published |
| **I-4** | **Adaptation is routine, not exceptional** | Teams change their own working methods on a defined cadence without approval |

**What is [A] Adaptable:** who grants the authority and how; whether it is announced publicly or arranged privately; whether dissent flows in a meeting, a pre-meeting, a 1:1, or a written channel; how error is discussed; the pace of adoption; the vocabulary.

**What is [L] Local:** language, ceremony, symbols, meeting formats, recognition mechanisms, training delivery, local naming of the programme.

> **Design implication:** the programme should have a local name in most markets. A single global brand name is a vanity, not a requirement. What must be global is I-1 to I-4 and the measurement of them.

---

## §2 Empowerment is not the opposite of hierarchy

The most common HQ error is to assume the initiative requires flattening. It does not. In high-power-distance environments, **autonomy that is not explicitly and visibly granted by a senior figure is not autonomy — it is a trap**, and employees correctly read it as such.

| Environment | How empowerment is *created* | How it is *destroyed* |
|---|---|---|
| **Low power distance** (Nordics, NL, ANZ, IL, parts of US/UK) | Remove approval steps; clarify accountability; increase decision *speed* | Adding consultation; ambiguity about who finally decides |
| **High power distance** (much of Asia, LatAm, Gulf, parts of Southern/Eastern Europe) | Senior leader publicly and specifically delegates, names the scope, and is seen to defend the delegate's decision | Delegating quietly; overruling the delegate in public; delegating without budget or headcount |

In the second column, hierarchy is the *instrument* of empowerment. The senior leader's authority is spent to purchase the junior's autonomy. Asking a high-power-distance organisation to "just be less hierarchical" removes the only mechanism available.

---

## §3 The five variables that actually predict what to do

Rather than a country list, diagnose each site on five dimensions. These are the ones that change the intervention.

| Variable | Question | If HIGH → | If LOW → |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Power distance** | Would a junior person contradict a senior in an open meeting? | Delegate explicitly and publicly; use senior air cover; collect dissent in 1:1s and pre-meetings | Clarify final accountability; reduce consultation; speed up |
| **2. Directness of disagreement** | Is "no" said, implied, or routed through a third party? | Direct debate is engagement, not conflict — train HQ not to read it as resistance | Build indirect channels; train managers to hear silence, hedging and delay as dissent |
| **3. Uncertainty tolerance** | Will people act without a documented rule? | Pilot fast and iterate | Publish the concept, the rules, the boundaries and the FAQ *before* asking for behaviour change |
| **4. Task vs. relationship trust** | Is trust earned by competence or by relationship? | Credential the programme through expertise and evidence | Credential it through the personal sponsorship of trusted individuals |
| **5. Consequence memory** | What happened last time someone spoke up or failed? | Address history explicitly before asking for I-2/I-3 | Move faster |

Variable 5 is the strongest single predictor and is site-specific, not national. Do not skip it. In any site that has had a restructuring, a whistleblowing incident, or a punished failure in the last 24 months, I-2 and I-3 cannot be achieved by messaging; only by a demonstrated counter-example (§9.3).

---

## §4 The mandatory local diagnostic (before any rollout)

**[I] Invariant process, [L] local execution.** Each region completes this before launch. Two to three weeks; not a survey exercise.

1. **Decision archaeology.** Take five real decisions from the last quarter. Map who *actually* decided, how many approvals, elapsed time. This gives the true baseline, not the org chart.
2. **Escalation audit.** Count what escalated and why. Sort into: (a) genuinely needed seniority, (b) risk-avoidance, (c) no one knew who owned it. (b) and (c) are the addressable mass.
3. **Middle-manager interviews.** 10–15 managers: *"What decision would you like to make that you currently can't? What would go wrong if you did?"*
4. **Language test.** Have the core messages translated by a local employee, then back-translated by another. Discard any term whose back-translation carries abandonment, demotion, or extra unpaid work.
5. **Constraint scan.** Works councils, unions, employment law, data/monitoring law, nationalisation quotas (§8).
6. **Consequence history.** What happened to the last person who publicly disagreed with local senior leadership? Everyone knows the answer; ask until you get it.

**Output:** a two-page regional adaptation memo stating the five variable scores, the translated vocabulary, the constraints, and the three highest-value first moves. HQ reviews for coherence with I-1 to I-4 — **not** for stylistic conformity to HQ.

---

## §5 Regional starting hypotheses

Read with the caveat in §0.3. "Watch for" = the characteristic way the initiative fails in that setting.

### 5.1 Northern & Western Europe

| Region | Likely reception | Do | Watch for |

1. **The request centres on leadership; the draft is mostly about programme design.** There is almost nothing on: how regional leaders are *selected* for this; what capability they need and how it is built; coaching/peer mechanisms across regions; what happens when the Regional President is himself the blocker (the single most common cause of regional non-adoption); expatriate vs. local leadership credibility. "Success depends on effective leadership across all regional offices" is the user's premise, and the draft never addresses leader capability or leader accountability directly.

2. **Middle managers are diagnosed but not solved for.** §1 correctly identifies "your manager's authority is being reduced" as a status threat that "mobilises the exact layer we depend on." The document then interviews that layer (§4.3) and never returns. There is no re-contracting of the middle-manager role, no answer to what they *gain*, no protection of their status, no change to how they are evaluated. This is the largest single omission in the surviving text.

3. **No HR systems alignment.** You cannot produce I-1 to I-4 while promotion criteria, performance ratings, incentive design and succession still reward escalation, compliance and zero-defect records. Behaviour follows the reward system, not the guidance note. Nothing on this.

A global culture initiative fails in one of two symmetrical ways:

| Failure | Mechanism | Symptom at month 9 |
|---|---|---|
| **Over-standardisation** | HQ exports its own cultural idiom as if it were the change itself | Perfect compliance in the HQ region, polite non-adoption everywhere else |
| **Over-localisation** | Every region redefines "empowerment" until it means whatever it was already doing | Twelve programmes, one name, no transferable capability |

The defence against both is to decide *in advance* which elements are fixed globally and which are deliberately delegated. Everything in this document is therefore tagged:

| Tag | Meaning | Who decides | Change process |
|---|---|---|---|
| **[I] Invariant** | Identical everywhere. Non-negotiable. | Executive Sponsor | Board-level exception only |
| **[A] Adaptable** | The *outcome* is fixed; the *method* is regional | Regional President, with HQ visibility | Documented, not requested |
| **[L] Local** | Wholly delegated to the country/site | Country leader | No approval needed |

If a leader cannot say which of the three a given element is, the element is not ready to roll out.

### 0.2 The resourcing rule

**Every commitment made to this initiative consumes manager attention, and manager attention is already fully allocated.** No new behaviour is introduced anywhere in this programme without naming what stops, what is deferred, or what budget replaces it. Section 12 enforces this numerically. A workstream with no stated displacement cost has not been designed; it has been wished for.

### 0.3 A caution on the regional material in §5

The regional profiles are **starting hypotheses, not facts.** National-culture frameworks (Hofstede, GLOBE, Meyer) describe population averages and are prone to three errors when applied to a company:

1. **Ecological fallacy.** Within-country variation in management style usually exceeds between-country variation. A Munich R&D lab and a Munich sales office differ more than Munich and Milan R&D labs.
2. **Sample mismatch.** Our employees are not a national sample. They are urban, educated, English-capable, self-selected into a multinational, and in several markets a majority-expatriate workforce.
3. **Staleness.** Generational change in India, Korea, China, the Gulf and Poland has moved faster in fifteen years than these frameworks have.

Use §5 to form a question, then verify it locally in the diagnostic (§4). Treating §5 as settled truth reproduces exactly the stereotyping the initiative is meant to dissolve.

## §1 What "empowerment" must mean before it can be translated

The word is the first risk. In English, "empowerment" is a positive abstraction. Translated literally it frequently arrives as one of:

- *"You are now on your own"* — abandonment, especially where managerial protection is a valued part of the leadership contract
- *"Your manager's authority is being reduced"* — a status threat that mobilises the exact layer we depend on
- *"More work, same grade, same pay"* — offloading
- *"Another HQ campaign"* — where a decade of programmes has taught cynicism

Therefore the programme is defined **behaviourally, not lexically**. The following four outcomes are **[I] Invariant**; every regional expression must produce them, and no regional expression may substitute for them.

| # | Invariant outcome | Observable test |
|---|---|---|
| **I-1** | **Decision rights are explicit and pushed to the lowest competent level** | A named decision-rights map exists per team; ≥X% of a defined decision class is closed without escalation |
| **I-2** | **Disagreement can be surfaced upward without career cost** | Employees can name a recent instance where a decision changed because someone junior objected |
| **I-3** | **Honest error is survivable** | At least one visible case per region where a good-faith failure was reviewed without sanction, and the learning published |
| **I-4** | **Adaptation is routine, not exceptional** | Teams change their own working methods on a defined cadence without approval |

**What is [A] Adaptable:** who grants the authority and how; whether it is announced publicly or arranged privately; whether dissent flows in a meeting, a pre-meeting, a 1:1, or a written channel; how error is discussed; the pace of adoption; the vocabulary.

**What is [L] Local:** language, ceremony, symbols, meeting formats, recognition mechanisms, training delivery, local naming of the programme.

> **Design implication:** the programme should have a local name in most markets. A single global brand name is a vanity, not a requirement. What must be global is I-1 to I-4 and the measurement of them.

## §2 Empowerment is not the opposite of hierarchy

The most common HQ error is to assume the initiative requires flattening. It does not. In high-power-distance environments, **autonomy that is not explicitly and visibly granted by a senior figure is not autonomy — it is a trap**, and employees correctly read it as such.

| Environment | How empowerment is *created* | How it is *destroyed* |
|---|---|---|
| **Low power distance** (Nordics, NL, ANZ, IL, parts of US/UK) | Remove approval steps; clarify accountability; increase decision *speed* | Adding consultation; ambiguity about who finally decides |
| **High power distance** (much of Asia, LatAm, Gulf, parts of Southern/Eastern Europe) | Senior leader publicly and specifically delegates, names the scope, and is seen to defend the delegate's decision | Delegating quietly; overruling the delegate in public; delegating without budget or headcount |

In the second column, hierarchy is the *instrument* of empowerment. The senior leader's authority is spent to purchase the junior's autonomy. Asking a high-power-distance organisation to "just be less hierarchical" removes the only mechanism available.

## §3 The five variables that actually predict what to do

Rather than a country list, diagnose each site on five dimensions. These are the ones that change the intervention.

| Variable | Question | If HIGH → | If LOW → |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Power distance** | Would a junior person contradict a senior in an open meeting? | Delegate explicitly and publicly; use senior air cover; collect dissent in 1:1s and pre-meetings | Clarify final accountability; reduce consultation; speed up |
| **2. Directness of disagreement** | Is "no" said, implied, or routed through a third party? | Direct debate is engagement, not conflict — train HQ not to read it as resistance | Build indirect channels; train managers to hear silence, hedging and delay as dissent |
| **3. Uncertainty tolerance** | Will people act without a documented rule? | Pilot fast and iterate | Publish the concept, the rules, the boundaries and the FAQ *before* asking for behaviour change |
| **4. Task vs. relationship trust** | Is trust earned by competence or by relationship? | Credential the programme through expertise and evidence | Credential it through the personal sponsorship of trusted individuals |
| **5. Consequence memory** | What happened last time someone spoke up or failed? | Address history explicitly before asking for I-2/I-3 | Move faster |

Variable 5 is the strongest single predictor and is site-specific, not national. Do not skip it. In any site that has had a restructuring, a whistleblowing incident, or a punished failure in the last 24 months, I-2 and I-3 cannot be achieved by messaging; only by a demonstrated counter-example (§9.3).

## §4 The mandatory local diagnostic (before any rollout)

**[I] Invariant process, [L] local execution.** Each region completes this before launch. Two to three weeks; not a survey exercise.

1. **Decision archaeology.** Take five real decisions from the last quarter. Map who *actually* decided, how many approvals, elapsed time. This gives the true baseline, not the org chart.
2. **Escalation audit.** Count what escalated and why. Sort into: (a) genuinely needed seniority, (b) risk-avoidance, (c) no one knew who owned it. (b) and (c) are the addressable mass.
3. **Middle-manager interviews.** 10–15 managers: *"What decision would you like to make that you currently can't? What would go wrong if you did?"*
4. **Language test.** Have the core messages translated by a local employee, then back-translated by another. Discard any term whose back-translation carries abandonment, demotion, or extra unpaid work.
5. **Constraint scan.** Works councils, unions, employment law, data/monitoring law, nationalisation quotas (§8).
6. **Consequence history.** What happened to the last person who publicly disagreed with local senior leadership? Everyone knows the answer; ask until you get it.

**Output:** a two-page regional adaptation memo stating the five variable scores, the translated vocabulary, the constraints, and the three highest-value first moves. HQ reviews for coherence with I-1 to I-4 — **not** for stylistic conformity to HQ.

## The recommendation in one paragraph

A global empowerment initiative fails in two symmetrical ways: HQ exports its own cultural idiom as if the idiom were the change (perfect adoption at headquarters, polite non-adoption everywhere else), or every region redefines "empowerment" until it means what it was already doing (twelve programmes, one name, no transferable capability). The defence against both is to fix the **outcomes** globally and delegate the **methods** regionally, deciding which is which *before* rollout rather than arguing about it in month nine. We therefore define empowerment behaviourally, not lexically — four observable outcomes (§1) built on an explicit three-class decision-rights taxonomy — and treat everything else as adaptable or local. The central non-obvious point, which should reshape how most of our regional leaders act, is that **empowerment is not the opposite of hierarchy**: autonomy requires a visible, credible grantor, and in most of our markets the only person who can grant it is the senior figure being asked to "flatten" (§2). The second non-obvious point is that the strongest predictor of whether this works at a given site is not national culture but **local consequence memory** — what actually happened to the last person who disagreed or failed there (§3.1). Two populations decide the outcome and both are currently under-served by change programmes of this kind: **regional leaders**, who must be selected and held to a capability bar rather than merely briefed (§6), and **middle managers**, whose status is what the initiative appears to attack and who must therefore be re-contracted, not exhorted (§7). None of it survives contact with an unchanged reward system, so HR-systems alignment is invariant, not optional (§10). Two claims in this paper are load-bearing and are deliberately **not** asserted: that our Wave 1 sites have sufficient consequence-memory headroom for I-2 and I-3 to be achievable by messaging plus mechanism, and that our middle managers will accept the re-contract in §7 at the price offered. §15 states in advance what result would stop or de-scope the programme.

National-culture frameworks (Hofstede; the GLOBE studies; Erin Meyer's *The Culture Map*) are **descriptive heuristics with known and serious limits**, not predictive instruments:

- **Aggregation-level error.** Hofstede's dimensions were derived from a single-employer survey population (IBM, late 1960s–early 1970s) and describe country means. - **Staleness.** Generational change in India, Korea, Greater China, the Gulf and Central Europe has plausibly outrun the frameworks' vintage. Also **[R]**.

| **I-4** | **Adaptation is routine** | Team-level working-method change log | ≥[75]% of teams have changed at least one of their own working methods per quarter without upward approval, for two consecutive quarters |

### 1.3 The decision classes — the substance behind the slogan **[I] for the taxonomy, [A] for the thresholds**

Empowerment that does not name decisions is a poster. Three classes, defined globally; monetary thresholds indexed regionally by the Regional President within a ±[40]% band **[A]**:

| Class | Content | Devolution |
|---|---|---|
| **A — Reserved** | Safety; legal and regulatory commitments; capital above €[250]k; pricing outside approved band; external brand and sustainability claims; hiring above grade [M3]; anything creating precedent across regions | **Never devolved.** Naming these protects the rest. |
| **B — Devolvable (the whole target of I-1)** | Operating spend to €[25]k; method and process change within a team; supplier selection from the approved list; customer concession to €[10]k; scheduling and resourcing within budget; hiring to grade [M2] within approved plan; local vendor and tooling choices | **Devolved by named, written, publicly issued grant** (§9.2) |
| **C — Already local** | Anything a team already decides without asking | No action — but audit for shadow escalation |

I-1's test is deliberately *not* "a decision-rights map exists." Documentation measures documentation. The map (a Class B grant register per team) is a prerequisite; the measured outcome is the escalation rate found by decision archaeology.

### 1.4 Why I-3 is written as it is **[I]**

v1.0 required "one visible case per region where a good-faith failure was reviewed without sanction, and the learning published." That metric corrupts under pressure: regions would curate a harmless failure and publish it. It also collides with **[V]** limits on publishing employee-identifiable conduct reviews in Germany, France, the Netherlands and any EU jurisdiction under GDPR Art. 6/9, and with works-council rights where publication has disciplinary implication.

The rewrite measures the **leader's** behaviour and the **system's** response, not an exhibit:

- Every good-faith failure above a materiality line gets a review whose written output is **process and decision-focused, anonymised at individual level** — no names, no attributable conduct findings.
- Sanction data is audited in aggregate by Internal Audit **[I]**, not self-reported by the region.
- The one *personal* disclosure required is from the senior leader themselves — a leader's own account of a decision they got wrong. That is safe (the discloser holds the power), non-extractive, and it is the single most efficient signal available (§9.3).

### 1.5 What is not fixed

| Element | Tag |
|---|---|
| Who grants authority, how visibly, in what forum | **[A]** |
| Whether dissent flows in the meeting, the pre-meeting, a 1:1, or in writing | **[A]** |
| How error is discussed, and by whom | **[A]** |
| Pace of adoption within the Gate schedule (§13) | **[A]** |
| Vocabulary, programme name, translation | **[L]** |
| Ceremony, symbols, recognition mechanisms, training delivery format | **[L]** |

> **Design implication:** most markets should give the programme a **local name**. A single global brand name is a vanity. What must be global is I-1 to I-4, the decision classes, and the measurement.

---

## §2 Empowerment is not the opposite of hierarchy **[I] as a principle**

The most common HQ error is to assume the initiative requires flattening. It does not — and in much of the company, flattening would remove the only available instrument.

**The mechanism, stated generally:** autonomy is only usable if the person exercising it believes it will be **defended**. Belief requires a **grantor** who is (a) visible, (b) credible to that employee, and (c) seen to bear the cost when a delegated decision goes wrong. Three variables follow, and they are what actually differ between our sites — not "how hierarchical people are":

| Variable of the grant | Range observed | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **Who is a credible grantor** | The direct manager / the site's senior figure / a respected technical authority / the works council or union as co-signatory / a visible HQ sponsor | Grant issued by the wrong figure is not believed and will not be used |
| **How visible the grant must be** | Private confirmation is sufficient ↔ public, specific, named announcement is required | Where public grant is required, quiet delegation reads as a trap and employees correctly decline it |
| **How the grantor's cost-bearing is demonstrated** | Verbal support ↔ the grantor publicly absorbs the first failure | Undemonstrated cost-bearing collapses the grant on first error |

Where a public, specific grant is required, **hierarchy is the instrument of empowerment**: the senior leader's authority is spent to purchase the junior's autonomy. Telling such an organisation to "just be less hierarchical" is asking it to destroy the mechanism and call the rubble progress.

Three failure modes are universal **[I] to avoid**: delegating without budget or headcount; overruling the delegate in public; and re-absorbing the decision quietly after the announcement. Any one of them ends I-1 at that site regardless of what the survey says.
